extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and designers of monumental buildings
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for composing architectural surfaces by masses of light and shade, choice and treatment of materials, traceries, and ornament so as to achieve breadth, dignity, and true monumental effect. Focuses on how an architect should plan forms in relation to light, shadow, curvature, and subordinate ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer rough blocks for greater height/economy
rubrics_metrics.description: “the labour and time necessary to do this would be better spent in another way; and that to raise a building to a height of a hundred feet with rough blocks, is better than to raise it to seventy with smooth ones.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material and workmanship economically: favour mass and height achieved with rougher, bolder masonry over smaller-scale refinement that sacrifices scale and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the natural cleavage and character of stone
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is also a magnificence in the natural cleavage of the stone to which the art must indeed be great that pretends to be equivalent”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-polishing or disguising the stone's innate qualities; seek a ‘brotherhood with the mountain heart’ rather than 'glistering obedience' to artificial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide surface into masses of light and shade or traced hues
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those divisions are necessarily, either into masses of light and shade, or else by traced hues”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the primary divisions of a wall or surface by broad masses of light and dark (or by deliberate traced color) rather than by fussy, small-scale ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat wall surface like a canvas but with higher sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: “a wall surface is to an architect simply what a white canvass is to a painter, with this only difference, that the wall has already a sublimity in its height, substance, and other characters… on which it is more dangerous to break than to touch”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when breaking the plane of a wall—respect its inherent grandeur and avoid small-scale interventions that undermine its sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive shade is essential and sublime in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: “positive shade is a more necessary and more sublime thing in an architect's hands than in a painter's”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definite, deep shadows as principal means of architectural expression; light alone cannot supply the architect's ‘rests’ or chief sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think in shadow — design for actual lighting conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “one of the first habits that a young architect should learn, is that of thinking in shadow… conceiving it as it will be when the dawn lights it, and the dusk leaves it”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive forms as they will appear in morning and evening, consider heat/cold effects and how shadows will fall and fade; design with the dynamics of real light in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead along lights and cut out shadows with intention
rubrics_metrics.description: “let him cut out the shadows, as men dig wells… and lead along the lights, as a founder does his hot metal; let him keep the full command of both”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control both light and shadow deliberately—shape shadow as a carved element and lead eye-movement with luminous planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure masses of light and darkness are broad, bold, and deep
rubrics_metrics.description: “spaces of light and darkness… the one is broad and bold enough not to be swallowed up by twilight, and the other deep enough not to be dried like a shallow pool by a noon-day sun.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thin, shallow modelling; ensure light areas hold up against ambient light and shadow areas retain depth across lighting conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throw quantities of shade/light into masses (breadth law)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the first necessity is that the quantities of shade or light… shall be thrown into masses, either of something like equal weight, or else large masses of the one relieved with small of the other; but masses of one or other kind there must be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose designs by clear large-scale masses rather than myriad small parts; balanced or contrasted massing is fundamental to majestic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'mass' (form-bearing) from 'interval' (field)
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is convenient sometimes to restrict the term 'mass' to the portions to which proper form belongs, and to call the field on which such forms are traced, interval.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ‘masses’ for elements carrying form and ‘intervals’ as the background fields—this distinction clarifies composition and treatment of ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal mass styles: light (rounded/gradation) vs dark (flat/sharp)
rubrics_metrics.description: “one in which the forms are drawn with light upon darkness… the other in which they are drawn with darkness upon light… the use of the dark mass characterises… a trenchant style… the use of the light mass… associated with a softened and full manner”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether forms read as lights on dark fields (rounded, graded, soft) or dark forms on light fields (flat, sharply edged); each implies different moulding, edge treatment, and overall character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounded masses: aim for gradation and readableness
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Greek workman cared for shadow only as a dark field wherfrom his light figure or design might be intelligibly detached: his attention was concentrated on the one aim at readableness, and clearness of accent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with rounded, light-centred masses, favour gradation and clarity; ornament and detail must not obscure the primary readable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine/rounded approach: diffusion of light for grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Byzantine light and shade are as incontestably more grand and masculine, based on that quality of pure gradation, which nearly all natural objects possess”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use smooth gradations and rounded masses to emulate natural grandeur (clouds, mountains, tree-heads) when a monumental, embracing character is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve serenity on plane and curved surfaces; avoid intrusive ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: “the desirableness of serenity in plane surfaces… applies still more forcibly to those which are curved… serenity and power may be carried into minor divisions”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain calmness and breadth on large planes and curved forms; subordinate decorative work must not break the serenity of these surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature necessary in small masses to secure grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: “curvature of some degree there must be, in order to secure any measure of grandeur in a small mass of light.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce slight curvature in small lit masses so they read as rounded, monumental forms rather than flat, trivial details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design traceries by dark forms first; mark black spots for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “the composition of the whole depends on the proportioning and shaping of the darks… it is quite useless to draw Italian tracery in outline; if with any intention of rendering its effect, it is better to mark the black spots, and let the rest alone.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing or designing tracery, prioritize the dark penetrations that create the pattern; treat intermediate ornament as subordinate or omit it for clear effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage stained glass carefully—glass often spoils tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: “glass spoils all traceries; and it is much to be wished that it should be kept well within them, when it cannot be dispensed with”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open traceries where possible; if glazing is necessary, set the glass back behind the stone so it does not destroy the intended black/white shadow pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penetrative (pierced) ornaments: cut deep and keep bold independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “in the northern architect… he had no resource but to cover his walls with holes, cut into foiled shapes… cut so deep in every case, as to secure… great breadth of shadow… For some time the penetrative ornaments… maintained their bold and independent character. Then they multiplied and enlarged, becoming shallower as they did so; then they began to run together… finally, they lost their individual character altogether.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pierced ornament as strong, independent dark forms—avoid multiplying them until they become shallow, merged, and lose power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep ornament subordinate; retain purity of shadow-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “No knots of flowerwork, no ornaments of any kind, were suffered to interfere with the purity of its form… so that the quatrefoil… told upon the eye, with all its four black leaves, miles away.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament should not compete with the principal masses or shadow-forms; simplify or withdraw secondary decoration to maintain clarity at distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mouldings: prefer broad surfaces; beware fillet/edge growth destroying gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those of the earlier times were… composed of alternate square and cylindrical shafts… the eye in all cases dwells on broad surfaces… a low ridgy process is seen emerging… it grows and pushes out… until the roll itself becomes subordinate to it”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mouldings to preserve broad gradation; avoid the accretion of fillets and sharp ridges that create distracting edges and destroy smooth tonal gradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek breadth (flatness or gradation) as primary quality; avoid substitution by mere hue
rubrics_metrics.description: “gradation in the one, flatness in the other, and breadth in both, being the qualities sought and exhibited… up to the period when… the hue was substituted for the mass”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize compositional breadth—either by smooth gradation (rounded masses) or by flat dark masses—rather than relying on color alone to divide surfaces.
